concepts.prompt: What is the practical difference between an array-backed list (e.g. C++ vector/Java ArrayList) and a linked structure, in terms of what operations you reach for?
expectedConcepts: contiguous memory gives O(1) random access
linked structures give O(1) insert/delete at a known node
choose based on access pattern, not habit

concepts.prompt: When does using an unordered/hash-based collection change your algorithm's complexity class versus a sorted/tree-based one?
expectedConcepts: hash map/set: average O(1) lookup, no ordering guarantee
tree map/set: O(log n) lookup, sorted iteration
pick hash for existence/count, tree when order or range queries matter

concepts.prompt: What is the difference between buffered and unbuffered I/O, and why does it matter for competitive-style problems reading large input?
expectedConcepts: unbuffered per-token I/O is slow at scale
buffering/fast IO reduces syscalls
sync_with_stdio(false) / BufferedReader class of fixes

concepts.prompt: Why do pass-by-value vs pass-by-reference semantics matter when writing recursive or in-place mutating functions?
expectedConcepts: value copies isolate mutation from caller
reference/pointer sharing lets a function mutate caller state
unintentional copying silently breaks in-place algorithms

concepts.prompt: What is integer overflow and in which common DSA operations does it silently produce wrong answers?
expectedConcepts: fixed-width integer wraps past its max
common in sum-of-array, multiplication, mid = (l+r)/2
fix: wider type, or mid = l + (r-l)/2

concepts.prompt: What's the practical difference between a shallow copy and a deep copy of a data structure, and when does it bite you?
expectedConcepts: shallow copy duplicates the top-level container only
nested references still point to the original objects
matters for cloning graphs/linked structures/nested arrays

concepts.prompt: What two loop variables control a printed shape, and what does each typically represent?
expectedConcepts: outer loop controls row/level
inner loop controls column/character within the row
the relationship between them defines the shape

concepts.prompt: How do you derive the inner loop's bound as a function of the outer loop's current value for a triangular pattern?
expectedConcepts: express spaces or characters per row as a formula in terms of the row index
test the formula on row 1 and the last row first
off-by-one errors are the dominant bug source here

concepts.prompt: What is the general technique for printing a symmetric (e.g. pyramid or diamond) pattern using space + character counts per row?
expectedConcepts: compute leading spaces and characters separately per row
diamond = increasing half + decreasing half
reuse the increasing-row function twice, mirrored

concepts.prompt: Why is it useful to mentally separate 'what to print' from 'how many times to print it' when designing a new pattern?
expectedConcepts: decouples the character/content logic from the loop-bound logic
makes it easy to adapt one pattern's loop structure to a new pattern's content

concepts.prompt: What's a common off-by-one mistake when converting a 1-indexed row description into 0-indexed loop counters?
expectedConcepts: forgetting to adjust the bound when switching between i<n and i<=n
row 'n' in problem statement vs loop variable ending at n-1

concepts.prompt: How do you extract and process individual digits of a number without converting it to a string?
expectedConcepts: repeatedly take n % 10 for the last digit, n /= 10 to remove it
loop while n > 0 (or handle n=0 specially)

concepts.prompt: What is the Euclidean algorithm for GCD, and how does it derive LCM?
expectedConcepts: gcd(a,b) = gcd(b, a%b), base case gcd(a,0)=a
lcm(a,b) = a*b / gcd(a,b)
runs in O(log(min(a,b)))

concepts.prompt: How do you check primality efficiently, and why is checking divisors up to sqrt(n) sufficient?
expectedConcepts: if n has a factor > sqrt(n), it has a paired factor < sqrt(n)
checking up to sqrt(n) covers all factor pairs
gives O(sqrt n) per check

concepts.prompt: What is the difference between a number's divisors and its prime factorization, and how do you compute prime factorization efficiently?
expectedConcepts: divisors: all numbers dividing n; prime factors: the irreducible multiplicative building blocks
trial-divide by increasing i while i*i<=n, dividing out each factor fully

concepts.prompt: Why does modular arithmetic matter in problems asking for an answer 'mod 1e9+7', and what operations does it distribute over?
expectedConcepts: prevents overflow on huge results
distributes over + and *, not directly over - or / (needs modular inverse for division)

concepts.prompt: What problem does a frequency map solve that a plain array can't, in general?
expectedConcepts: counts occurrences of arbitrary/sparse keys, not just small dense integer ranges
array counting only works when the key space is small and known

concepts.prompt: When is it better to use a fixed-size array as a counting structure instead of a hash map?
expectedConcepts: when keys are bounded and small (e.g. lowercase letters, digits 0-9)
array indexing avoids hashing overhead and gives guaranteed O(1)

concepts.prompt: What is the general recipe for solving 'find pair/triplet with property X' using a hash set in one pass?
expectedConcepts: as you scan, check whether the complement/required partner has already been seen
insert current element after checking, to avoid using an element with itself

concepts.prompt: Why is a hash map's O(1) lookup an *average* case rather than a guarantee, and what causes the degradation?
expectedConcepts: collisions force multiple keys into the same bucket
worst case degrades toward O(n) when many keys collide
good hash functions and resizing keep collisions rare in practice

concepts.prompt: What must be true about a type before it can be used as a hash map key?
expectedConcepts: it must have a stable hash and a consistent equality definition
mutating a key after insertion corrupts lookups because its bucket no longer matches its hash

concepts.prompt: What is the general strategy for a puzzle-style problem where brute enumeration is too slow: find structure, or find invariant?
expectedConcepts: look for what quantity stays constant or changes predictably across allowed moves
an invariant argument can prove impossibility without simulating

concepts.prompt: Why is working a puzzle backward (from the goal state) sometimes easier than forward simulation?
expectedConcepts: goal state often has fewer possible predecessors than the start state has successors
useful when forward branching factor is large

concepts.prompt: What is the pigeonhole principle, and what kind of DSA claim does it let you prove without construction?
expectedConcepts: if n items go into m < n containers, some container holds more than one item
proves existence of a duplicate/collision without finding it, e.g. duplicate in an array of n+1 values from 1..n

concepts.prompt: What is a parity argument, and how does it prove some puzzle configurations are unreachable?
expectedConcepts: track whether a quantity is odd or even across all legal moves
if every move preserves parity and the goal has different parity from the start, the goal is provably unreachable

concepts.prompt: Why is 'find a small counterexample' often a faster path than trying to prove an approach correct?
expectedConcepts: a single concrete failing case definitively kills a wrong approach
cheaper than constructing a proof, and it redirects effort before you invest in implementing something broken

concepts.prompt: What are the two mandatory components of any correct recursive function?
expectedConcepts: a base case that terminates without recursing
a recursive case that makes measurable progress toward the base case

concepts.prompt: Why must a recursive call's argument change in a way that provably approaches the base case?
expectedConcepts: otherwise the recursion never terminates and overflows the call stack
progress must be monotonic toward the base condition

concepts.prompt: What is the call stack doing during recursion, and how does that explain recursion's O(depth) space cost?
expectedConcepts: each call pushes a frame holding its locals and return address
frames stay live until that call returns
max simultaneous frames = max recursion depth

concepts.prompt: What causes a stack overflow in recursion, and roughly what recursion depth is typically safe?
expectedConcepts: each pending call consumes a stack frame; too many nested calls exhaust the stack
typically safe to a depth in the low tens of thousands; deeper needs iteration or an explicit stack

concepts.prompt: When should you convert a recursive solution to an iterative one, and what do you need to manage manually?
expectedConcepts: when recursion depth risks overflow or the call overhead matters
you must explicitly maintain the state that the call stack was implicitly holding, usually via your own stack

concepts.prompt: How do you determine a recursive function's space complexity separately from its time complexity?
expectedConcepts: space is driven by maximum recursion depth (frames alive simultaneously), not total number of calls made
a function making 2^n calls but only n deep uses O(n) stack space, not O(2^n)

concepts.prompt: What is the difference between parameterized and functional recursion, and when is an accumulator parameter necessary?
expectedConcepts: parameterized recursion threads extra state (accumulator) through the calls
functional recursion returns a value and combines results after the call returns
accumulator needed when you want O(1) extra work per level instead of combining afterward

concepts.prompt: Why can an accumulator-based recursive function sometimes be rewritten as an iterative loop (tail recursion), and why does that matter in languages without tail-call optimization?
expectedConcepts: if the recursive call is the last operation and state is fully carried in parameters, it's tail-recursive
without TCO the language still builds a full stack, so it's not free just because it's 'tail'

concepts.prompt: Why does threading state through parameters (rather than mutating a shared/global variable) make recursion easier to reason about?
expectedConcepts: each call's state is explicit and isolated in its own frame
avoids needing to undo shared mutations, which is the main source of subtle backtracking bugs

concepts.prompt: What is the difference between passing an accumulator by value versus by reference, and what bug does the wrong choice cause?
expectedConcepts: by value: each branch gets an independent copy, no cleanup needed
by reference: branches share one structure and require explicit undo after the recursive call, or sibling branches see corrupted state

concepts.prompt: How would you use a parameterized-recursion style to compute a running sum or path without returning values up the stack?
expectedConcepts: carry the running value as a parameter, adding to it before recursing
at the base case, record or output the accumulated result directly rather than combining return values

concepts.prompt: In divide-and-conquer recursion, what three steps does every solution follow?
expectedConcepts: divide the problem into subproblems
conquer (recurse) each subproblem
combine the subproblem results into the final answer

concepts.prompt: When a function makes multiple recursive calls per invocation (not just one), how do you reason about the total time complexity?
expectedConcepts: draw or count the recursion tree: branching factor per call times depth
T(n) = k*T(n/b) + f(n) style recurrences; use recursion tree or Master theorem intuition

concepts.prompt: What is the Master theorem's practical use for recurrences of the form T(n) = a*T(n/b) + f(n)?
expectedConcepts: compares the work done splitting/combining f(n) against the recursive work n^(log_b a)
whichever dominates determines the overall complexity, giving a quick answer without expanding the recursion tree by hand

concepts.prompt: Why do T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) and T(n) = 2T(n-1) + O(1) have wildly different complexities?
expectedConcepts: the first divides the input size (depth log n, O(n log n) total, e.g. merge sort)
the second decrements it (depth n with branching 2, giving O(2^n), e.g. naive subset enumeration)

concepts.prompt: What distinguishes a function that returns a value to be combined from one that mutates shared results, and why does that affect reusability?
expectedConcepts: a returning (functional) recursion is self-contained and composable, easy to memoize
a mutating recursion depends on external state, making it harder to test, reuse, or cache

concepts.prompt: How do you express 'process array from index i to end' recursively, and what is the base case?
expectedConcepts: pass the current index as state, recurse on i+1
base case: index reaches array length (or crosses the other pointer)

concepts.prompt: When solving an array problem with two pointers recursively (e.g. from both ends), what invariant keeps the recursion correct?
expectedConcepts: the two pointers must converge (progress toward each other) every call
base case is pointers meeting or crossing

concepts.prompt: How would you recursively reverse an array in place, and what is the base case?
expectedConcepts: swap arr[left] and arr[right], then recurse on (left+1, right-1)
base case: left >= right

concepts.prompt: How does recursive binary search on a sorted array differ structurally from linear recursion over the array?
expectedConcepts: binary search halves the range per call (depth O(log n)); linear recursion decrements the index (depth O(n))
the difference in how the range shrinks is what changes the complexity class

concepts.prompt: Why is passing array indices (start/end) preferable to slicing/copying subarrays in recursive array algorithms?
expectedConcepts: slicing copies O(n) elements per call, adding a hidden O(n) factor to every level
index passing keeps each call O(1) in extra space and preserves the intended complexity

concepts.prompt: Why is recursion a natural fit for string parsing problems (e.g. nested structures, expression parsing)?
expectedConcepts: strings often have self-similar/nested substructure
a substring problem is naturally a smaller instance of the same problem

concepts.prompt: What's the standard recursive check for whether a string is a palindrome using two pointers, and what's its base case?
expectedConcepts: compare s[left] and s[right]; if equal, recurse on left+1, right-1
base case: left >= right

concepts.prompt: How do you recursively generate all subsequences of a string, and what is the branching factor?
expectedConcepts: at each character, branch into include and exclude
branching factor 2 with depth n, giving 2^n subsequences

concepts.prompt: Why do string-recursion problems often prefer index-passing over creating substrings at each call?
expectedConcepts: substring creation is O(n) per call in most languages, multiplying the true complexity
passing an index keeps each level O(1)

concepts.prompt: What base case handles the empty string correctly, and why is it easy to get wrong?
expectedConcepts: base case should trigger when the index reaches the string length (which is immediately true for an empty string)
checking for length 1 instead silently breaks on empty input

concepts.prompt: What distinguishes plain recursion from backtracking?
expectedConcepts: backtracking explores a choice, recurses, then explicitly undoes the choice (state restoration) before trying the next option
plain recursion doesn't need to 'undo' shared mutable state

concepts.prompt: Why is explicit state restoration (undo the choice) required after a backtracking recursive call returns?
expectedConcepts: the same mutable structure (path, visited set) is reused across sibling branches
without undoing, later branches see stale state from an earlier branch

concepts.prompt: What three-step template do virtually all backtracking algorithms follow?
expectedConcepts: choose (make a move / add to path)
explore (recurse into the resulting state)
un-choose (undo the move before trying the next option)

concepts.prompt: How does adding a pruning condition to plain recursive enumeration turn it into practical backtracking?
expectedConcepts: a validity/feasibility check before recursing cuts off entire subtrees of the search space early
without pruning you enumerate everything, which is usually exponentially too slow

concepts.prompt: What is the difference between a decision tree's total nodes and the number of solutions found, and why does that matter for complexity estimates?
expectedConcepts: you may explore vastly more nodes than you ultimately produce solutions
complexity is driven by nodes visited, not answers returned, so pruning quality dominates real performance

concepts.prompt: What is the fundamental lower bound for comparison-based sorting, and why can't a comparison sort beat it?
expectedConcepts: Omega(n log n) comparisons in the worst case
based on the decision-tree argument: n! orderings need log2(n!) ~= n log n comparisons to distinguish

concepts.prompt: What's the difference between a stable and an unstable sort, and when does stability matter?
expectedConcepts: stable sort preserves relative order of equal-key elements
matters when sorting by one key but needing tie-order from a previous sort/insertion order to survive

concepts.prompt: Compare merge sort and quicksort: what do they trade off in the worst case and in extra space?
expectedConcepts: merge sort: guaranteed O(n log n), needs O(n) extra space, stable
quicksort: O(n log n) average but O(n^2) worst case (bad pivot), in-place, usually not stable

concepts.prompt: Why does a poor pivot choice degrade quicksort to O(n^2), and what mitigations exist?
expectedConcepts: consistently picking the smallest/largest element as pivot creates maximally unbalanced partitions
mitigations: randomized pivot, median-of-three, introsort fallback

concepts.prompt: When is a non-comparison sort (counting sort, radix sort) applicable, and why can it beat the n log n bound?
expectedConcepts: applicable when keys are integers in a known bounded range
it isn't comparison-based, so the n log n lower bound doesn't apply; runs in O(n+k)

concepts.prompt: How does merge sort count inversions in O(n log n) as a byproduct of merging?
expectedConcepts: during the merge step, when an element from the right half is taken before a remaining left-half element, all remaining left elements form inversions with it
add (mid - i + 1) to the inversion count at that step

concepts.prompt: What general class of counting/comparison problems can be solved by piggybacking on merge sort's merge step?
expectedConcepts: any 'count pairs (i<j) satisfying a condition comparable during merge' problem, e.g. inversions, reverse pairs, count pairs with sum/ratio condition

concepts.prompt: Why is the 'count while merging' trick correct only because both halves are already sorted at that point?
expectedConcepts: sortedness means when right[j] < left[i], it is also less than every remaining element of the left half
that lets you count many pairs at once instead of comparing individually

concepts.prompt: How would you adapt the merge-based counting technique for 'reverse pairs' where the condition is a[i] > 2*a[j]?
expectedConcepts: run a separate counting pass over both sorted halves before the actual merge, using a two-pointer scan with the modified condition
the merge itself stays unchanged; only the counting pass encodes the condition

concepts.prompt: What is the complexity of merge-sort-based counting, and why doesn't the extra counting pass change the asymptotic bound?
expectedConcepts: O(n log n) overall
the extra counting pass is O(n) per merge level, the same order as the merge itself, so it's absorbed

concepts.prompt: What is the general approach to 'simulate the process described in the problem' array questions, versus finding a closed-form shortcut?
expectedConcepts: simulation directly re-enacts the described process step by step
correct when the process is well-defined and n is small enough that direct simulation fits time limits

concepts.prompt: What is the Boyer-Moore Voting invariant, and why does it correctly find a majority element in O(n) time and O(1) space?
expectedConcepts: maintain a candidate and a count; a mismatch decrements, a match increments, count 0 means switch candidate
if a true majority (>n/2) element exists, it survives all cancellations because every other value can cancel at most one occurrence of it per pairing

concepts.prompt: What's the difference between generating the next permutation in-place versus generating all permutations recursively?
expectedConcepts: next-permutation finds the lexicographically next arrangement via a pivot/suffix-reverse technique in O(n), without enumerating all permutations
generating all permutations is inherently O(n!) and uses backtracking

concepts.prompt: How do you rotate an array in-place by k positions using O(1) extra space?
expectedConcepts: reverse the whole array, then reverse the first k and the remaining n-k separately (or equivalent 3-reversal trick)
avoids the O(n) extra array of a naive rotate

concepts.prompt: Why does a majority-element candidate found by Boyer-Moore Voting still need a verification pass in the general case?
expectedConcepts: the algorithm guarantees the correct answer only if a strict majority element actually exists
if none does, it still returns some candidate, so a second counting pass is needed to confirm

concepts.prompt: What is the general algorithm for computing the next lexicographic permutation in place?
expectedConcepts: scan from the right for the first index i where a[i] < a[i+1] (the pivot)
swap the pivot with the smallest element to its right that is still greater than it, then reverse the suffix after the pivot

concepts.prompt: What is the standard one-pass hash map technique for two-sum-style problems, and why is it O(n) instead of O(n^2)?
expectedConcepts: for each element, check if (target - element) already exists in the map before inserting current element
avoids the nested-loop pairwise check

concepts.prompt: How does the XOR trick find the single non-repeating element when every other element appears exactly twice?
expectedConcepts: XOR is commutative/associative and a^a=0, 0^a=a
XORing everything cancels all paired elements, leaving the unique one

concepts.prompt: When should you reach for a hash map over a frequency array for counting problems on arrays?
expectedConcepts: when the value range is large, negative, or sparse relative to n
array counting only works for small bounded non-negative ranges

concepts.prompt: Why does a hash-map approach to a pair-sum problem require inserting the current element *after* checking for its complement?
expectedConcepts: inserting first would let an element pair with itself when target is exactly 2*element
checking before inserting enforces that the two indices are distinct

concepts.prompt: When does sorting plus two pointers beat a hash map for pair/triplet-sum problems?
expectedConcepts: when you need O(1) extra space, or need to easily skip duplicate triplets
hash map wins when the array must stay unsorted or original indices are required in the answer

concepts.prompt: What does a prefix sum array let you compute in O(1) that would otherwise take O(n)?
expectedConcepts: the sum of any contiguous subarray, via prefix[r] - prefix[l-1]
trades O(n) preprocessing for O(1) range-sum queries

concepts.prompt: What is Kadane's algorithm's invariant for maximum subarray sum, and why is it correct to reset the running sum to 0 (or the current element) when it goes negative?
expectedConcepts: maintain the best sum ending at the current index
a negative running sum can only hurt any future extension, so dropping it and restarting is never worse

concepts.prompt: How do you count subarrays with a given sum K using prefix sums and a hash map, in O(n)?
expectedConcepts: track frequency of each prefix sum seen so far; for current prefix P, add freq[P - K] to the answer
relies on prefix[r] - prefix[l] = K being equivalent to a hash lookup

concepts.prompt: Why does the XOR-prefix technique generalize the sum-prefix technique for 'subarray with XOR = K' problems?
expectedConcepts: XOR prefix satisfies the same telescoping property as sum: xorPrefix[l..r] = xorPrefix[0..r] ^ xorPrefix[0..l-1]
same hash-map-of-seen-prefixes trick applies, replacing subtraction with XOR

concepts.prompt: Why is a hash map of prefix sums necessary for 'count subarrays with sum K' when the array can contain negatives, whereas a sliding window suffices when all values are positive?
expectedConcepts: with only positive values the running sum is monotonic as the window grows, so shrinking/expanding is well-defined
with negatives the sum isn't monotonic, so a window can't decide which direction to move; prefix-sum hashing doesn't rely on monotonicity

concepts.prompt: How does a 2D prefix sum let you compute the sum of any submatrix in O(1), and what is the inclusion-exclusion formula?
expectedConcepts: precompute prefix[i][j] = sum of the rectangle from (0,0) to (i,j)
submatrix sum = prefix[r2][c2] - prefix[r1-1][c2] - prefix[r2][c1-1] + prefix[r1-1][c1-1] (adding back the doubly-subtracted corner)

concepts.prompt: What initialization does the prefix-sum hash map need before the scan begins, and what breaks without it?
expectedConcepts: insert prefix sum 0 with count 1 before scanning
without it, subarrays starting at index 0 that already equal K are never counted

concepts.prompt: What precondition does the classic 'same direction' or 'opposite ends' two-pointer technique usually require on the input?
expectedConcepts: typically requires the array to be sorted (or monotonic in the relevant property)
without sortedness, moving a pointer can't be justified as never missing a better answer

concepts.prompt: What is the Dutch National Flag invariant for a 3-way partition (e.g. sort 0s/1s/2s)?
expectedConcepts: maintain three regions: [0,low) all 'low' value, [low,mid) all 'mid' value, [high+1,n) all 'high' value, [mid,high] unknown
swap and advance pointers based on the current element's category, shrinking the unknown region

concepts.prompt: Why does the two-pointer merge technique (as in merging two sorted arrays) run in O(n+m) instead of O(n*m)?
expectedConcepts: both pointers only move forward, each pointer advances at most n or m times total
no element is revisited, so total work is linear in combined size

concepts.prompt: Why can't the opposite-ends two-pointer technique be applied to an unsorted array for a pair-sum problem?
expectedConcepts: moving a pointer inward is justified only because it monotonically increases or decreases the sum
without sortedness there's no guarantee moving inward improves anything, so valid pairs get skipped

concepts.prompt: What is the 'same direction' (slow/fast writer-reader) two-pointer technique used for, and give the shape of the invariant?
expectedConcepts: in-place filtering/compaction, e.g. remove duplicates or move zeros
invariant: everything before the slow pointer is already finalized and correct; the fast pointer scans for the next element that belongs there

concepts.prompt: How do you avoid emitting duplicate triplets in a sorted-array 3-sum solution?
expectedConcepts: after fixing or moving a pointer, skip forward over any values equal to the one just used at that position
requires the array to be sorted so duplicates are adjacent

concepts.prompt: What signal in a problem statement tells you a sliding window applies, and what disqualifies it?
expectedConcepts: looking for a contiguous subarray/substring satisfying some property
answer/property changes monotonically as the window grows or shrinks
disqualified when valid elements can be non-contiguous (that's a subsequence/DP problem)

concepts.prompt: What's the difference between a fixed-size and a variable-size sliding window?
expectedConcepts: fixed-size: window length is a given constant k, slide by adding one and removing one each step
variable-size: window grows/shrinks based on a validity condition, size is not predetermined

concepts.prompt: In a variable-size window, what specifically triggers expanding the right edge versus shrinking the left edge?
expectedConcepts: expand right to include more elements while the window is still valid or too small
shrink left when the window violates the constraint (e.g. too many distinct chars, sum too large)

concepts.prompt: What invariant must a sliding window maintain at all times for the technique to be correct?
expectedConcepts: the window always represents a valid candidate range (or the current expand/shrink state) consistent with what's being tracked (sum, count map, distinct count)
auxiliary state (running sum/frequency map) must stay in sync with the actual left/right bounds

concepts.prompt: What is the typical time complexity of a sliding window solution over an array of size n, and why isn't it O(n^2) despite nested-looking logic?
expectedConcepts: O(n) because each pointer (left and right) moves forward at most n times total across the whole run
amortized analysis: total shrink operations across the whole algorithm are bounded by n

concepts.prompt: When does sliding window NOT apply even though the problem statement mentions 'subarray'?
expectedConcepts: when elements can be negative and you need a window sum condition that isn't monotonic as you shrink/expand (e.g. arbitrary negative numbers break monotonic sum window)
use prefix sum + hashmap instead in that case

concepts.prompt: What is the standard first step before applying most interval algorithms, and why is it necessary?
expectedConcepts: sort intervals by start time (or sometimes end time)
without sorting, you can't make a linear greedy pass and correctly decide overlap in one direction

concepts.prompt: What is the precise condition for two intervals to overlap, and how does that generalize to merging a sorted list of intervals?
expectedConcepts: intervals [a,b] and [c,d] overlap if a <= d and c <= b (equivalently, next.start <= current.end after sorting by start)
merging: walk sorted intervals, extend the current merged interval's end while next.start <= current.end, else start a new merged interval

concepts.prompt: For 'find the minimum number of meeting rooms / maximum overlap' style problems, why is sorting starts and ends separately (or using a heap) better than pairwise overlap checks?
expectedConcepts: you only need the count of currently active intervals, not which specific ones overlap
a sweep over sorted start/end events gives O(n log n) instead of O(n^2) pairwise checks

concepts.prompt: When should you sort intervals by END time rather than START time?
expectedConcepts: when greedily selecting the maximum number of non-overlapping intervals (activity selection)
sorting by end leaves the most remaining room for future picks; sorting by start does not give that guarantee

concepts.prompt: What edge cases must interval problems explicitly define before implementation?
expectedConcepts: whether touching endpoints (e.g. [1,2] and [2,3]) count as overlapping
empty input, single interval, and fully nested intervals

concepts.prompt: What's the general technique for traversing a matrix in spiral order without an explicit visited array?
expectedConcepts: maintain four shrinking boundaries: top, bottom, left, right; traverse each side then shrink the corresponding boundary
terminate when top>bottom or left>right

concepts.prompt: How do you rotate an N x N matrix 90 degrees in-place using O(1) extra space?
expectedConcepts: transpose the matrix (swap element[i][j] with element[j][i]), then reverse each row (or column, depending on direction)
two O(n^2) passes, no extra matrix needed

concepts.prompt: What is the standard technique for setting entire rows/columns to zero in-place when a cell is zero, using O(1) extra space?
expectedConcepts: use the matrix's own first row and first column as marker storage for which rows/columns to zero
handle the first row and first column themselves separately with two scalar flags, since they double as the markers

concepts.prompt: How do you search a matrix sorted row-wise and column-wise (but not globally flattenable) in O(n+m)?
expectedConcepts: start at the top-right (or bottom-left) corner; moving left decreases the value, moving down increases it
each comparison eliminates a full row or column

concepts.prompt: What index arithmetic converts a flat index into (row, col) for an R x C matrix, and when is that flattening valid for binary search?
expectedConcepts: row = idx / C, col = idx % C
valid only when the whole matrix is globally sorted in row-major order (each row's last element <= the next row's first)

concepts.prompt: What is the precondition binary search always requires on the search space, and why does violating it break correctness?
expectedConcepts: the search space must be monotonic with respect to the predicate being tested (sorted, or 'true...true false...false' shaped)
without monotonicity, discarding half the space can discard the answer

concepts.prompt: How do you adapt 1D binary search to search a 2D matrix that is row-wise and column-wise sorted, in O(log(n*m))?
expectedConcepts: treat the matrix as a flattened sorted array; convert a single mid index to (row, col) via mid/cols and mid%cols
requires each row's last element <= next row's first element for full flattening to be valid

concepts.prompt: Why is mid = low + (high - low) / 2 preferred over mid = (low + high) / 2?
expectedConcepts: (low + high) can overflow a fixed-width integer for large indices
the subtraction form computes the same midpoint without overflow risk

concepts.prompt: What determines whether a binary search loop should use while (low <= high) versus while (low < high), and what bug does mixing them cause?
expectedConcepts: low <= high with mid+1/mid-1 updates suits exact-match search; low < high with a converging update suits boundary-finding
mixing the condition with the wrong update rule causes either an infinite loop or a skipped candidate

concepts.prompt: What is binary search's space complexity iteratively versus recursively?
expectedConcepts: O(1) iteratively
O(log n) recursively due to the call stack

concepts.prompt: What does 'lower bound' mean precisely, and how does the binary search loop invariant differ from a classic exact-match search?
expectedConcepts: lower bound = first index whose value is >= target (leftmost valid position)
instead of stopping on equality, keep narrowing right when arr[mid] >= target and record mid as a candidate answer, then search left half for an earlier one

concepts.prompt: How do you use lower_bound to answer 'first and last occurrence of a target' and 'floor of a value'?
expectedConcepts: first occurrence = lower_bound(target) if it equals target
floor = lower_bound(target) minus one position if arr[lb] != target (or lb-1 directly)

concepts.prompt: Why does a boundary-finding binary search record a candidate answer instead of returning immediately on a match?
expectedConcepts: an earlier valid index may still exist to the left, so it must keep searching that side
returning on first match gives an arbitrary matching index, not the leftmost one

concepts.prompt: What should lower_bound return when the target is greater than every element in the array, and why is that convention useful?
expectedConcepts: it returns the array's length (a one-past-the-end index)
the convention makes it directly usable as an insertion position without a special case

concepts.prompt: How do you use lower_bound to find the correct insertion position that keeps an array sorted?
expectedConcepts: lower_bound(target) is exactly the leftmost index where the target can be inserted while preserving order

concepts.prompt: What is the precise difference between upper bound and lower bound, and how does that change the comparison in the loop?
expectedConcepts: upper bound = first index whose value is strictly > target
lower bound uses >= target; upper bound uses > target as the narrowing condition

concepts.prompt: How do you compute 'count of elements equal to target' using upper_bound and lower_bound together?
expectedConcepts: count = upperBound(target) - lowerBound(target)
works because both bounds delimit exactly the equal-to-target range

concepts.prompt: How is upper_bound used to compute the 'ceil' or the last occurrence of a value?
expectedConcepts: last occurrence = upperBound(target) - 1, valid only if that index holds the target
ceil of a value is lowerBound(value); upperBound gives the first strictly-greater element

concepts.prompt: What does upper_bound return when the target is absent from the array, and why is that the same as lower_bound in that case?
expectedConcepts: it returns the index of the first element greater than the target
when no element equals the target, no index satisfies '== target', so >= and > select the same position

concepts.prompt: Why do upper_bound and lower_bound both run in O(log n) despite finding different boundaries?
expectedConcepts: both halve the search space each iteration; only the comparison predicate differs, not the number of iterations

concepts.prompt: In a rotated sorted array, how do you decide which half is 'properly sorted' at each step, and why does that let you binary search?
expectedConcepts: compare arr[low] with arr[mid]: whichever side satisfies arr[low] <= arr[mid] (or arr[mid] <= arr[high]) is the sorted half
check if target lies within that sorted half's range to decide which half to recurse into

concepts.prompt: What's the general technique for finding a 'peak element' (element greater than both neighbours) in O(log n)?
expectedConcepts: compare arr[mid] with arr[mid+1]; if increasing, a peak must exist to the right (or mid+1 itself), else search left
relies on the fact a peak is guaranteed to exist given boundary conditions treated as -infinity

concepts.prompt: Why can XOR-based or bitwise search spaces (e.g. single element in doubled array) sometimes be binary-searched even without a simple sorted order?
expectedConcepts: exploit a different monotonic property, e.g. pairing parity of indices before/after the single element shifts
the predicate 'is the answer to the left or right of mid' must still be a clean boolean split

concepts.prompt: In a rotated sorted array containing duplicates, why does the standard 'which half is sorted' check break, and what is the fallback?
expectedConcepts: when arr[low], arr[mid], and arr[high] are all equal you cannot tell which half is sorted
shrink the bounds by one on each side and continue, degrading the worst case to O(n)

concepts.prompt: How do you find the index of the minimum element (the rotation pivot) in a rotated sorted array?
expectedConcepts: compare arr[mid] with arr[high]: if arr[mid] > arr[high] the minimum is strictly right of mid, otherwise it is at mid or left of it
converge until low == high

concepts.prompt: Why does the 'single element in a sorted doubled array' problem admit binary search, given the array isn't sorted by the property you're searching for?
expectedConcepts: before the unique element, pairs start at even indices; after it, pairs start at odd indices
that index-parity flip is the monotonic predicate binary search needs

concepts.prompt: What is the core idea of 'binary search on the answer', as opposed to binary searching over the input array directly?
expectedConcepts: binary search over the space of *possible answers* (e.g. a capacity, a speed, a max value), using a feasibility check function
requires the feasibility predicate to be monotonic: if X works, every value beyond X in the same direction also works

concepts.prompt: What must be true about the feasibility/check function for binary search on answer to be valid?
expectedConcepts: it must be monotonic (a boolean 'is this candidate answer feasible' that flips exactly once across the search range)
if feasibility isn't monotonic, binary search silently gives a wrong answer with no error

concepts.prompt: What is the general difference between 'minimize the maximum' and 'maximize the minimum' binary-search-on-answer problems, in how the check function and search direction are set up?
expectedConcepts: minimize max: check(x) = 'can we achieve max <= x', search for smallest feasible x
maximize min: check(x) = 'can we achieve min >= x', search for largest feasible x
direction of narrowing (move left/right on success) flips between the two

concepts.prompt: Why is the overall complexity of binary-search-on-answer typically O(check_cost * log(range)), and why does that beat brute force?
expectedConcepts: each candidate answer costs one feasibility check, and log(range) candidates are tried
brute force would test every value in the answer range individually

concepts.prompt: What are the two things you must define explicitly before writing any binary-search-on-answer solution?
expectedConcepts: the search range: the minimum and maximum plausible answers
the feasibility predicate: a function that returns whether a given candidate answer is achievable

concepts.prompt: How do you choose the lower and upper bounds of the answer space, and what happens if the bounds are too narrow?
expectedConcepts: lower bound is usually the largest single element or a trivial minimum; upper bound is usually the total sum or a trivial maximum
if the true answer falls outside the chosen range, the search returns a bound instead of the answer, with no error raised

concepts.prompt: How do you verify your feasibility function is actually monotonic before trusting the result?
expectedConcepts: check that once check(x) is true, check(x+1) (or check(x-1), depending on direction) is also true for the whole remaining range
brute-force the predicate across a small range and confirm it flips exactly once

concepts.prompt: What is the key idea behind finding the median of two sorted arrays in O(log(min(n,m))) using binary search on a partition?
expectedConcepts: binary search for a partition point in the smaller array such that elements on the left of both partitions are all <= elements on the right of both partitions
median is derived from the boundary elements of that valid partition, not by merging

concepts.prompt: Why does binary searching the smaller of the two arrays (not the larger) matter for correctness and complexity?
expectedConcepts: the partition of the second array is derived from the first array's partition and total length; searching the smaller array keeps the derived partition always valid
gives O(log(min(n,m))) instead of O(log(max(n,m)))

concepts.prompt: What condition defines a valid partition when finding the median of two sorted arrays, in terms of the four boundary elements?
expectedConcepts: maxLeftA <= minRightB and maxLeftB <= minRightA
when both hold, everything on the left side is <= everything on the right side across both arrays combined

concepts.prompt: How do you handle the boundary cases where a partition puts zero elements or all elements on one side?
expectedConcepts: treat the missing left boundary as -infinity and the missing right boundary as +infinity
this makes the comparison conditions hold automatically without special-case branching

concepts.prompt: How does the median-partition technique generalize to finding the Kth element of two sorted arrays?
expectedConcepts: instead of partitioning at the combined midpoint, partition so that exactly K elements fall on the left side
the same boundary-validity condition applies, only the target partition size changes

concepts.prompt: Why is a string best treated as an immutable value in some languages, and what performance trap does that create in a loop?
expectedConcepts: in languages like Java/Python, string concatenation in a loop can be O(n) per operation, O(n^2) total
fix: use a mutable buffer (StringBuilder, list + join) and build once

concepts.prompt: What's the standard technique for in-place reversal or manipulation of a string when the language allows mutable char arrays?
expectedConcepts: convert to a mutable array (or use two pointers directly), swap symmetric positions, convert back if needed

concepts.prompt: What is the difference between a character's ASCII/Unicode code point and its index in the string, and where does that distinction cause bugs?
expectedConcepts: a code point is the character's numeric value; the index is its position
bugs appear when using c - 'a' as an array index without checking the character is actually a lowercase letter

concepts.prompt: Why does the O(26) frequency-array trick assume something about the input alphabet, and what breaks it?
expectedConcepts: it assumes only lowercase English letters
mixed case, digits, spaces, or Unicode overflow or misindex the array

concepts.prompt: What's the technique for removing or compressing characters in a string in-place using two pointers?
expectedConcepts: a read pointer scans forward while a write pointer marks the next output position
everything before the write pointer is finalized output; the final string length is the write pointer's ending position

concepts.prompt: What is the standard O(n) check for whether two strings are anagrams, and why is sorting both strings (O(n log n)) a worse alternative?
expectedConcepts: build a frequency count (array of 26 or hash map) for one string, decrement while scanning the other, check all zero at the end
sorting works but is asymptotically worse when a linear frequency check suffices

concepts.prompt: How do you group a list of strings into anagram groups efficiently?
expectedConcepts: use a canonical key per string (sorted characters, or a fixed-length frequency signature) and group by that key in a hash map

concepts.prompt: Why is a fixed-length frequency signature usually a better anagram-group key than the sorted string?
expectedConcepts: building the signature is O(n) per string; sorting is O(n log n)
matters when strings are long, though sorting is simpler and fine for short strings

concepts.prompt: How do you find all anagram occurrences of a pattern within a longer string efficiently?
expectedConcepts: slide a fixed-size window equal to the pattern's length, maintaining a running frequency count
compare the window's counts against the pattern's counts at each position, updating incrementally instead of recounting

concepts.prompt: What edge cases must an anagram check handle before comparing frequency counts?
expectedConcepts: strings of different lengths can never be anagrams (check first and exit early)
empty strings, and whether case and whitespace are significant

concepts.prompt: What's the general strategy for parsing a numeral or numeric string with sign, whitespace, and overflow edge cases (e.g. atoi-style problems)?
expectedConcepts: explicitly handle stages in order: skip whitespace, read optional sign, read digits while valid, clamp on overflow
treat it as a state machine rather than ad hoc conditionals to avoid missed edge cases

concepts.prompt: Why do parsing problems require careful boundary/edge-case enumeration up front, rather than discovering them via test failures?
expectedConcepts: parsing bugs are almost always missed edge cases (empty string, only sign, leading zeros, overflow) not algorithmic errors
enumerating cases first avoids an unstructured trial-and-error fix loop

concepts.prompt: How do you detect integer overflow while parsing digits, before it actually happens?
expectedConcepts: before appending a digit, check whether the accumulated value already exceeds (MAX - digit) / 10
checking after the fact is too late because the overflow has already wrapped

concepts.prompt: What is the standard approach for parsing Roman numerals, and what rule handles subtractive pairs like IV and IX?
expectedConcepts: scan left to right; if the current symbol's value is less than the next symbol's value, subtract it, otherwise add it
this single rule covers all subtractive pairs without enumerating them

concepts.prompt: Why is treating a parsing problem as an explicit ordered sequence of stages more reliable than a chain of ad hoc conditionals?
expectedConcepts: stages make the valid ordering (whitespace, sign, digits, trailing junk) explicit and each stage's job independent
ad hoc conditionals tend to miss combinations of edge cases that the staged form makes obvious

concepts.prompt: What is the 'expand around center' technique for finding the longest palindromic substring, and why does it need 2n-1 centers?
expectedConcepts: for each possible center, expand outward while characters match
odd-length palindromes center on a character, even-length center between two characters, giving 2n-1 total centers

concepts.prompt: What is the time complexity of expand-around-center, and how does Manacher's algorithm improve on it?
expectedConcepts: expand-around-center: O(n^2) worst case (n centers, each expansion up to O(n))
Manacher's reuses previously computed palindrome radii to achieve O(n)

concepts.prompt: Why does expand-around-center need to run twice per position (once for odd, once for even length)?
expectedConcepts: odd-length palindromes are centered on a single character; even-length ones are centered between two characters
handling only one case silently misses half of all possible palindromes

concepts.prompt: What's the difference between the longest palindromic SUBSTRING and the longest palindromic SUBSEQUENCE, and why do they need different techniques?
expectedConcepts: substring must be contiguous (expand-around-center or Manacher's applies)
subsequence need not be contiguous, which makes it a DP problem (LCS of the string and its reverse)

concepts.prompt: What is the two-pointer approach to checking a palindrome while ignoring non-alphanumeric characters and case?
expectedConcepts: move each pointer forward/backward past characters that should be ignored, then compare the normalized characters
advance both pointers only after a successful comparison

concepts.prompt: Why is a dummy/sentinel head node commonly used when a linked list operation might modify the actual head?
expectedConcepts: avoids special-casing 'is this the head node' in insert/delete logic
lets uniform code handle the first node the same as any other

concepts.prompt: What's the key structural difference between a singly and a doubly linked list, and what operation does that difference make O(1) instead of O(n)?
expectedConcepts: doubly linked list nodes hold both next and prev pointers
makes backward traversal and deletion-given-a-node O(1) without needing to find the previous node by scanning

concepts.prompt: What is the standard safe pattern for deleting a node from a singly linked list, and why do you need the previous node?
expectedConcepts: you must rewire prev.next to curr.next, which requires holding a reference to prev
track prev while traversing, or use a dummy head so the first node needs no special case

concepts.prompt: Why can't you compute a linked list's length in O(1) like an array's, and what does that force in algorithm design?
expectedConcepts: nodes are scattered with no index or stored count, so length requires a full O(n) traversal
forces single-pass techniques (two pointers) when you'd otherwise want length up front

concepts.prompt: What edge cases must every linked list operation handle before anything else?
expectedConcepts: empty list (head is null)
single-node list
operating on the head node itself

concepts.prompt: What are the three pointers needed to reverse a singly linked list iteratively, and what does each one track?
expectedConcepts: prev (already-reversed portion's head), curr (node being processed), next (saved before curr's pointer is overwritten)
at each step: save next, point curr.next to prev, advance prev and curr

concepts.prompt: How does recursive linked list reversal work, and what is its space complexity compared to the iterative version?
expectedConcepts: recurse to the end of the list first, then rewire pointers on the way back up (head.next.next = head; head.next = null)
O(n) recursion stack space, versus O(1) for the iterative version

concepts.prompt: Why must you save the next pointer before rewiring curr.next during iterative reversal?
expectedConcepts: overwriting curr.next destroys the only reference to the rest of the list
without saving it first, the remainder of the list is unreachable and lost

concepts.prompt: What is the time and space complexity of iterative linked list reversal, and why is it optimal?
expectedConcepts: O(n) time, O(1) space
every node must be visited at least once to rewire it, and only three pointers are needed regardless of list size

concepts.prompt: How do you reverse only a sublist between positions m and n, and what must be reconnected afterward?
expectedConcepts: traverse to the node before m, reverse the m..n segment, then reconnect: the pre-m node points to the new segment head, and the old segment head points to the node after n
a dummy head avoids special-casing m = 1

concepts.prompt: What is the tortoise-and-hare technique for finding a linked list's middle in one pass without knowing its length in advance?
expectedConcepts: slow pointer moves one step, fast pointer moves two steps per iteration
when fast reaches the end, slow is at the middle

concepts.prompt: Why does the tortoise-and-hare technique need careful handling of even- vs odd-length lists to define 'the middle' consistently?
expectedConcepts: fast reaching null vs fast.next reaching null distinguishes odd/even length and determines whether slow lands on the first or second middle node

concepts.prompt: Why is the two-pointer middle-finding technique better than counting length and then traversing halfway?
expectedConcepts: it needs one pass instead of two
matters when the list can only be traversed once, or in a streaming context

concepts.prompt: What loop condition do you use for fast/slow when you want the FIRST middle of an even-length list versus the SECOND?
expectedConcepts: while (fast.next != null && fast.next.next != null) lands slow on the first middle
while (fast != null && fast.next != null) lands slow on the second middle

concepts.prompt: What other problems reuse the fast/slow middle-finding step as a building block?
expectedConcepts: palindrome check (split then reverse the second half)
merge sort on a linked list (split step)
reordering a list (split, reverse, interleave)

concepts.prompt: How do you find the Nth node from the end of a linked list in one pass using two pointers?
expectedConcepts: advance one pointer N steps first, then move both pointers together until the lead pointer hits the end
the trailing pointer is now at the Nth-from-end node

concepts.prompt: What is the two-pointer technique for checking whether a linked list is a palindrome, in O(n) time and O(1) extra space?
expectedConcepts: find the middle (fast/slow), reverse the second half in place, compare first half against reversed second half
optionally restore the list afterward if mutation isn't allowed

concepts.prompt: How do you find the intersection node of two linked lists (possibly different lengths) using two pointers in O(n) without extra space?
expectedConcepts: walk both pointers; when one reaches the end, redirect it to the other list's head; they meet at the intersection (or both reach null simultaneously if none)
this equalizes the effective traversal distance without explicitly computing length difference

concepts.prompt: What is the general shape of the fast/slow pointer technique, and what determines the gap between the pointers?
expectedConcepts: either a fixed offset (one pointer starts N ahead) or a fixed speed ratio (one moves twice as fast)
the gap is chosen so that when the lead pointer terminates, the trailing pointer is exactly at the target position

concepts.prompt: Why does the Nth-from-end technique need a dummy head node when N equals the list's length?
expectedConcepts: that case means removing the actual head, and the trailing pointer would need to point 'before' the head
a dummy head gives it a valid node to hold

concepts.prompt: Why does Floyd's cycle detection (slow/fast pointers) guarantee slow and fast will meet if a cycle exists?
expectedConcepts: once both pointers are inside the cycle, the fast pointer gains on the slow pointer by 1 node per step, so it must eventually lap and meet it
the relative distance between them modulo cycle length shrinks by 1 each iteration

concepts.prompt: After detecting a cycle with slow/fast pointers, how do you find the exact starting node of the cycle?
expectedConcepts: reset one pointer to head, keep the other at the meeting point, advance both one step at a time; they meet at the cycle's start
correctness follows from the distance relationship between head-to-cycle-start and meeting-point-to-cycle-start

concepts.prompt: How do you compute the length of a cycle once it's detected?
expectedConcepts: from the meeting point, keep advancing one pointer and counting steps until it returns to the same node

concepts.prompt: Why can't you use a visited-set approach for cycle detection when the problem requires O(1) space?
expectedConcepts: a hash set of visited nodes is O(n) space
Floyd's two-pointer method achieves the same detection in O(1) space

concepts.prompt: What is the time complexity of Floyd's cycle detection, and why isn't it worse than O(n) despite pointers looping?
expectedConcepts: O(n)
the slow pointer travels at most the full list length before the fast pointer catches it, since fast closes the gap by one node per step

concepts.prompt: What's the technique for merging two sorted linked lists in O(n+m) time and O(1) extra space (excluding output pointers)?
expectedConcepts: use a dummy head, repeatedly attach the smaller of the two current nodes, advance that list's pointer
attach the remaining nodes of whichever list isn't exhausted first

concepts.prompt: How does merge sort generalize from arrays to linked lists, and what changes about the 'split' step?
expectedConcepts: split step uses slow/fast pointers to find the middle instead of index arithmetic (no random access)
merge step is the same sorted-merge logic as arrays

concepts.prompt: Why is a dummy head node especially valuable in merge operations?
expectedConcepts: it removes the need to special-case choosing the very first output node
the real result is simply dummy.next at the end

concepts.prompt: How do you merge K sorted linked lists efficiently, and what's the complexity of the heap approach versus pairwise merging?
expectedConcepts: heap of the K current heads: O(N log K)
naive sequential merging of one list at a time: O(N*K); divide-and-conquer pairwise merging also gives O(N log K)

concepts.prompt: Why is merge sort generally preferred over quicksort for linked lists?
expectedConcepts: merge sort needs only sequential access, which linked lists provide naturally, and it needs no extra array
quicksort relies on efficient random access for partitioning, which linked lists lack

concepts.prompt: What is the general recursive structure for reversing a linked list in groups of K?
expectedConcepts: reverse the first K nodes (checking at least K nodes exist first), then recursively process the rest and attach
the original head of each K-group becomes the tail, connecting to the next group's reversed head

concepts.prompt: What edge case must be handled if the remaining nodes at the end are fewer than K, and how does the answer differ based on the problem's requirement?
expectedConcepts: some variants leave the leftover group unreversed; others require reversing only if a full group exists
must count remaining nodes before deciding whether to reverse the final partial group

concepts.prompt: Why must you verify that K nodes remain BEFORE starting to reverse a group?
expectedConcepts: if fewer than K remain and the problem requires leaving them as-is, reversing them produces a wrong answer
checking after the fact would require undoing the reversal

concepts.prompt: What is the time and space complexity of K-group reversal done iteratively versus recursively?
expectedConcepts: both O(n) time since each node is rewired a constant number of times
iterative is O(1) space; recursive is O(n/K) stack space

concepts.prompt: Which node becomes the connection point between one reversed group and the next?
expectedConcepts: the original head of each group becomes that group's tail after reversal, so it is what links to the next group's new head

concepts.prompt: Why does an LRU cache require both a hash map and a doubly linked list, rather than either alone?
expectedConcepts: hash map gives O(1) key lookup; doubly linked list gives O(1) removal/reinsertion at the front/back to track recency
a list alone would need O(n) to find a key; a map alone can't track order cheaply

concepts.prompt: On a 'get' or 'put' operation in an LRU cache, what two things must happen to the linked list to maintain the recency invariant?
expectedConcepts: move the accessed/inserted node to the most-recently-used end
if over capacity, evict the node at the least-recently-used end

concepts.prompt: What is the complexity requirement that forces the hash-map-plus-doubly-linked-list design, rather than a simpler structure?
expectedConcepts: both get and put must be O(1)
any single structure forces one of the two operations to O(n): a list can't look up by key quickly, a map can't track recency order

concepts.prompt: Why does an LRU cache use a DOUBLY linked list rather than a singly linked one?
expectedConcepts: removing an arbitrary node in O(1) requires knowing its predecessor, which the prev pointer provides directly
a singly linked list would need an O(n) scan to find the predecessor

concepts.prompt: How does an LFU (least frequently used) cache differ from LRU in what it tracks and evicts?
expectedConcepts: LFU evicts by access count rather than recency, and needs frequency buckets plus a tie-break rule (usually LRU within the same frequency)
strictly more bookkeeping than LRU

concepts.prompt: What is the O(n) time, O(1) extra-space technique for deep-copying a linked list with random pointers, and why is a naive hash-map approach O(n) space instead?
expectedConcepts: interleave cloned nodes directly after their originals, set clone.random from original.random.next (the clone of the random target), then detach the interleaved list into two
hash map approach stores original-to-clone mapping explicitly, using O(n) extra space instead of using the list structure itself

concepts.prompt: What makes deep-copying a list with random pointers harder than copying a plain linked list?
expectedConcepts: a random pointer may target a node that hasn't been cloned yet
you need a way to map each original node to its clone before you can wire up random pointers

concepts.prompt: What are the three phases of the O(1)-space interleaving approach for deep-copying a random-pointer list?
expectedConcepts: phase 1: insert each clone directly after its original
phase 2: set clone.random = original.random.next
phase 3: detach the two interleaved lists, restoring the original

concepts.prompt: Why is restoring the original list's structure in phase 3 not optional?
expectedConcepts: the input must not be left mutated; callers still hold references to it
skipping restoration leaves the original list corrupted with interleaved clone nodes

concepts.prompt: What is the complexity of the interleaving approach versus the hash-map approach?
expectedConcepts: both O(n) time
interleaving is O(1) extra space; the hash map is O(n) extra space

concepts.prompt: What do the bitwise operators AND, OR, XOR, NOT, left-shift, right-shift each represent conceptually, not just syntactically?
expectedConcepts: AND: keep only bits set in both; OR: keep bits set in either; XOR: bits set in exactly one; shifts: multiply/divide by powers of 2

concepts.prompt: How do you check, set, clear, and toggle the i-th bit of a number using bitwise operators?
expectedConcepts: check: (n >> i) & 1; set: n | (1 << i); clear: n & ~(1 << i); toggle: n ^ (1 << i)

concepts.prompt: What does n & (n-1) compute, and what is it used for?
expectedConcepts: clears the lowest set bit of n
used to count set bits (Brian Kernighan's algorithm) or check if n is a power of two (n & (n-1) == 0)

concepts.prompt: Why should you use unsigned types or logical right shift when manipulating bits, and what goes wrong otherwise?
expectedConcepts: arithmetic right shift on a negative signed integer copies the sign bit, filling with 1s instead of 0s
this causes infinite loops in bit-counting code that shifts until the value becomes zero

concepts.prompt: How do you swap two numbers using XOR without a temporary variable, and what edge case breaks it?
expectedConcepts: a ^= b; b ^= a; a ^= b
breaks when both operands are the same memory location, which zeroes the value

concepts.prompt: What does n & -n compute, and how does that relate to n & (n-1)?
expectedConcepts: n & -n isolates the lowest set bit (returns just that bit)
n & (n-1) clears it; the two are complementary operations on the same bit

concepts.prompt: What three algebraic properties of XOR make it useful for 'find the unique element' problems?
expectedConcepts: a ^ a = 0 (self-cancelling)
a ^ 0 = a (identity)
commutative and associative, so order of XORing doesn't matter

concepts.prompt: How do you find two unique numbers when every other number appears exactly twice (the 'single number II/III' family)?
expectedConcepts: XOR everything to get x = a^b (the two uniques XORed together)
find any set bit in x to partition all numbers into two groups differing at that bit, then XOR each group separately

concepts.prompt: What is bitmask enumeration, and why is it a natural way to represent subsets in problems with a small number of elements (typically n <= ~20)?
expectedConcepts: each subset of n elements maps to an integer 0..2^n-1 where bit i indicates element i's presence
lets you enumerate all subsets via a simple loop, and use bitwise ops to add/remove/check elements in O(1)

concepts.prompt: How do you find the missing number in an array containing 0..n with exactly one value absent, using XOR?
expectedConcepts: XOR all array elements together with all values 0..n
every present value cancels itself, leaving only the missing one

concepts.prompt: Why does the XOR-partition step in the 'two unique numbers' problem work regardless of which set bit you choose?
expectedConcepts: any set bit in a^b is a position where a and b differ, so partitioning by that bit necessarily separates them
each duplicate pair still lands in the same partition and cancels

concepts.prompt: What is the complexity of iterating all subsets via bitmask enumeration, and what practical n does that limit you to?
expectedConcepts: O(2^n) subsets, or O(2^n * n) if you inspect every element of each subset
practical only up to roughly n = 20-25

concepts.prompt: How does fast exponentiation (binary exponentiation) compute a^b in O(log b) instead of O(b)?
expectedConcepts: decompose the exponent into binary; square the base each step and multiply the result in only when the corresponding bit is set
halves the exponent each iteration, giving logarithmic multiplications

concepts.prompt: How is bit manipulation used to enumerate or test divisor/prime-related properties efficiently in some problems?
expectedConcepts: e.g. using bitset-based sieve for primes, or representing divisibility/parity constraints as bitmask states in DP

concepts.prompt: What is the Sieve of Eratosthenes, and what is its time complexity?
expectedConcepts: mark multiples of each prime as composite, starting from p*p, up to n
O(n log log n), far better than testing each number individually

concepts.prompt: Why does the sieve start marking from p*p rather than from 2*p?
expectedConcepts: all smaller multiples of p were already marked by smaller prime factors
starting at p*p avoids redundant work without missing anything

concepts.prompt: How does modular exponentiation avoid overflow while computing large powers under a modulus?
expectedConcepts: apply the modulus after every multiplication rather than only at the end
keeps intermediate values bounded, relying on modular arithmetic distributing over multiplication

concepts.prompt: What is the standard recursive template for generating all subsets (the power set) of a set, and how does it branch?
expectedConcepts: at each element, branch into two recursive calls: include it, or exclude it
base case: reached end of input, add current subset to results

concepts.prompt: When the input has duplicate elements, what extra step avoids generating duplicate subsets?
expectedConcepts: sort the input first, then at each recursion level skip a candidate if it equals the previous sibling candidate already tried at this level
prevents re-exploring an identical branch

concepts.prompt: What is the time and space complexity of generating all subsets of n elements, and why is it unavoidable?
expectedConcepts: O(2^n * n) time (2^n subsets, each up to n elements to copy) and O(n) recursion depth
unavoidable because the output itself has 2^n entries

concepts.prompt: How does the iterative bitmask approach to subsets compare with the recursive include/exclude approach?
expectedConcepts: bitmask: loop 0..2^n-1, include element i when bit i is set — no recursion, easy to reason about
recursive: cleaner for adding pruning or handling duplicates via level-skipping

concepts.prompt: Why must the input be SORTED before the duplicate-skipping rule works?
expectedConcepts: the rule skips a candidate equal to the previous sibling, which requires equal values to be adjacent
on unsorted input, duplicates are separated and the skip never triggers

concepts.prompt: What's the difference between a subsequence and a substring/subarray, and why does that change which technique (backtracking vs sliding window) applies?
expectedConcepts: a subsequence preserves relative order but need not be contiguous; substring/subarray must be contiguous
non-contiguous choice-per-element naturally maps to include/exclude backtracking, not a window

concepts.prompt: What is the standard recursive structure for finding all subsequences that sum to a target K?
expectedConcepts: at each index, branch into 'include current element' and 'exclude it', tracking running sum and path
base case: index reaches end, check if running sum equals K

concepts.prompt: What is the recursion depth and branching factor for subsequence generation, and what total complexity does that give?
expectedConcepts: depth n (one level per element), branching factor 2 (include/exclude)
O(2^n) leaves, so O(2^n * n) with output copying

concepts.prompt: How does 'print any ONE subsequence with sum K' differ in implementation from 'print ALL of them'?
expectedConcepts: return a boolean from the recursion and stop exploring as soon as one succeeds
the early return prunes the entire remaining search space, unlike the all-solutions version

concepts.prompt: Why is counting subsequences with a given sum usually solved by DP rather than backtracking, once n grows?
expectedConcepts: backtracking is O(2^n); the subproblems (index, remaining sum) overlap heavily
memoizing them gives pseudo-polynomial O(n * sum) instead

concepts.prompt: What invariant keeps the standard combinations backtracking template from generating duplicate combinations (e.g. [1,2] and [2,1] as the same set)?
expectedConcepts: only recurse forward from the current index (never revisit earlier indices), enforcing an increasing order within each combination

concepts.prompt: What's the backtracking approach for generating all valid combinations of balanced parentheses?
expectedConcepts: track counts of open and close brackets used; only add '(' if open < n, only add ')' if close < open
base case: length reaches 2n

concepts.prompt: What is the difference between a permutation and a combination, and how does the recursive template differ for each?
expectedConcepts: combinations ignore order; permutations count orderings as distinct
combinations recurse forward from the current index only; permutations iterate over all unused elements with a used[] marker

concepts.prompt: In the balanced-parentheses generator, why is 'only add a close bracket if close < open' the sufficient validity rule?
expectedConcepts: it guarantees you never close a bracket that was never opened, which is exactly the balance invariant
combined with capping opens at n, every generated string is valid by construction — no post-filtering needed

concepts.prompt: How does phone-number letter-combination generation map digits to a branching structure?
expectedConcepts: each digit position is one recursion level; the branching factor is the number of letters that digit maps to
total combinations are the product of the per-digit letter counts

concepts.prompt: What is the difference between the 'unbounded' and 'bounded'/'fixed-size' variants of combination sum, and how does the recursion change?
expectedConcepts: unbounded: an element can be reused, so the recursive call stays at the same index when including it
bounded/no-reuse: recursive call must move to index+1 after including an element

concepts.prompt: How do you prune the combination-sum search space early instead of exploring every branch to completion?
expectedConcepts: sort candidates first, and stop the loop early once the running sum plus current candidate exceeds the target (since all later candidates are even larger)

concepts.prompt: When duplicates are allowed in the input but the answer set must not contain duplicate combinations, what technique prevents that?
expectedConcepts: sort input, then at each recursion level skip a candidate equal to the immediately preceding sibling candidate already tried at that level

concepts.prompt: What is the recursion-depth risk in unbounded combination sum, and how does the target bound it?
expectedConcepts: reusing the smallest candidate repeatedly gives depth up to target / min(candidate)
the target value, not the input size, bounds the depth

concepts.prompt: Why does sorting candidates enable an early break rather than just a continue in the loop?
expectedConcepts: once one candidate exceeds the remaining target, every later candidate is larger and also exceeds it
so you can exit the loop entirely instead of skipping one branch

concepts.prompt: What is the general backtracking template for constraint satisfaction: choose, explore, un-choose?
expectedConcepts: make a choice, recurse into the resulting state, and if that path fails or after it's explored, revert the choice before trying the next option
explicit undo keeps sibling branches independent

concepts.prompt: Why does pruning (checking constraint validity before recursing further, not after) dramatically improve backtracking performance?
expectedConcepts: invalid states are cut off immediately instead of being fully explored to a dead end
reduces the effective branching factor early, which compounds exponentially over depth

concepts.prompt: In graph coloring by backtracking, what is checked before assigning a color to a node, and why does that keep the search correct?
expectedConcepts: check that no adjacent node already has the same color before assigning it
ensures every partial coloring explored is a valid partial solution, not just any guess

concepts.prompt: What is the difference between backtracking and brute-force enumeration, given both explore the search space?
expectedConcepts: backtracking abandons a partial candidate as soon as it can't possibly extend to a solution
brute force builds every complete candidate first and only then tests validity

concepts.prompt: How does the palindrome-partitioning problem combine backtracking with a validity check at each split?
expectedConcepts: try every prefix as the next partition, but recurse only when that prefix is itself a palindrome
the palindrome check is the pruning condition that keeps the search tractable

concepts.prompt: What three conditions must be checked before placing a queen at a given cell, and how can each be tracked in O(1) instead of rescanning the board?
expectedConcepts: same column, same diagonal (row-col constant), same anti-diagonal (row+col constant)
track each with a boolean array/set indexed by column, (row-col+n), and (row+col) respectively

concepts.prompt: Why does placing queens row by row (one queen per row) reduce the search space compared to trying arbitrary cell-by-cell placement?
expectedConcepts: guarantees no two queens share a row by construction, cutting one whole class of conflicts out of the search entirely

concepts.prompt: What is the approximate complexity of N-Queens with and without the O(1) conflict checks?
expectedConcepts: worst case remains exponential (roughly O(N!)) in both
the O(1) checks remove an O(N) factor per placement, which matters a lot in practice

concepts.prompt: Why is (row - col + N) used as the diagonal index rather than (row - col)?
expectedConcepts: row - col can be negative, which is not a valid array index
adding N shifts the range into non-negative territory

concepts.prompt: What must be undone when backtracking from a queen placement?
expectedConcepts: clear the column, diagonal, and anti-diagonal markers set for that queen, and remove it from the board/path
leaving any marker set makes later sibling branches falsely see a conflict

concepts.prompt: What is the backtracking strategy for solving Sudoku, and what three constraints must be validated before placing a digit?
expectedConcepts: find an empty cell, try digits 1-9, recurse; backtrack if no digit leads to a solution
check the digit doesn't already appear in the same row, column, or 3x3 box

concepts.prompt: How can precomputed row/column/box 'used digit' sets speed up Sudoku backtracking versus rescanning the grid on every placement check?
expectedConcepts: maintain boolean sets per row, column, and box updated incrementally as digits are placed/removed
turns each validity check into O(1) instead of O(9) or more

concepts.prompt: How do you compute which 3x3 box a cell (row, col) belongs to?
expectedConcepts: boxIndex = (row / 3) * 3 + (col / 3), using integer division

concepts.prompt: What is the difference between returning a boolean from the Sudoku recursion versus continuing to explore?
expectedConcepts: returning true on success stops immediately, since only one solution is needed
continuing would enumerate all valid solutions, which is far more expensive

concepts.prompt: What heuristic beyond plain backtracking can dramatically speed up Sudoku solving?
expectedConcepts: choose the empty cell with the fewest legal candidates next (most-constrained-variable heuristic)
it shrinks the branching factor early rather than deep in the tree

concepts.prompt: What is the backtracking + DFS approach for finding a word in a grid, and why is a visited marker required at each recursive step?
expectedConcepts: from each cell matching the current character, DFS in four directions for the next character
mark the cell visited before recursing and unmark it after, to prevent reusing the same cell twice in one path

concepts.prompt: What's a simple pruning technique that can speed up grid-based word search before starting the full DFS?
expectedConcepts: check character frequency in the grid against the word's required frequencies first; if the grid lacks enough of some character, skip entirely

concepts.prompt: What is the time complexity of grid word search, in terms of grid size and word length?
