if chars match: dp[i][j]=dp[i-1][j-1]; else 1 + min(insert=dp[i][j-1], delete=dp[i-1][j], replace=dp[i-1][j-1])

concepts.prompt: What is the state and recurrence for Longest Common Subsequence, and how does it differ from the edit-distance recurrence?
expectedConcepts: dp[i][j] = LCS length of first i chars of A and first j chars of B
if chars match: dp[i][j] = 1 + dp[i-1][j-1]; else dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]) — no 'replace' cost, since LCS only cares about matching, not converting

concepts.prompt: How does the palindromic-subsequence family (e.g. longest palindromic subsequence) reduce to the LCS pattern?
expectedConcepts: longest palindromic subsequence of S equals the LCS of S and its reverse
reframes a seemingly different problem as an application of an already-solved pattern

concepts.prompt: What is the time and space complexity of the standard two-string DP, and how is space reduced?
expectedConcepts: O(n*m) time and O(n*m) space
reducible to O(min(n,m)) space by keeping only the previous row, though that sacrifices traceback for reconstruction

concepts.prompt: How do you reconstruct the actual LCS string, not just its length?
expectedConcepts: walk backward from dp[n][m]: on a character match step diagonally and prepend the character, otherwise move toward the larger neighbour
requires the full table, which is why space optimization blocks reconstruction

concepts.prompt: What is the general state-machine framing for stock-trading DP problems (holding vs not holding shares)?
expectedConcepts: define states per day like 'holding a share' and 'not holding a share' (sometimes with a cooldown/transaction-count dimension), and write transitions for buy/sell/hold actions between these states

concepts.prompt: How does allowing at most K transactions change the state space compared to the single-transaction or unlimited-transaction variants?
expectedConcepts: adds a transaction-count dimension to the state (day, transactions used, holding status)
single transaction: no transaction dimension needed; unlimited: greedy or a DP without a bounded count dimension suffices

concepts.prompt: Why does the unlimited-transactions variant admit a simple greedy solution while the K-transaction variant does not?
expectedConcepts: with unlimited transactions, capturing every upward price move is optimal and locally decidable
a transaction budget forces choosing WHICH moves to capture, which needs global comparison

concepts.prompt: How does a cooldown constraint change the state machine?
expectedConcepts: it adds a third state (in cooldown) between selling and being able to buy again
transitions must route through it rather than going directly from sold to buying

concepts.prompt: Where does a per-transaction fee enter the recurrence?
expectedConcepts: subtract it once per completed transaction, conventionally on the sell transition
applying it on both buy and sell would double-charge

concepts.prompt: What is the standard interval-DP recurrence shape for partition problems (choose a split point k inside a range), and why is it O(n^3) typically?
expectedConcepts: dp[i][j] = best result over range [i,j], computed by trying every split point k between i and j and combining dp[i][k] and dp[k+1][j]
O(n^2) ranges, each trying O(n) split points, gives O(n^3)

concepts.prompt: How does Matrix Chain Multiplication fit the interval-DP partition pattern, and what does dp[i][j] represent there?
expectedConcepts: dp[i][j] = minimum multiplication cost to fully parenthesize matrices i through j
transition tries every split point k, combining cost of multiplying (i..k) and (k+1..j) plus the cost of multiplying the two resulting matrices together

concepts.prompt: How do you identify a partition/interval DP problem from its statement?
expectedConcepts: the problem asks for an optimal way to split a sequence into contiguous groups, or to parenthesize/combine adjacent items
the cost of a group depends on the group as a whole, not on individual elements

concepts.prompt: Why must interval DP be filled in order of increasing interval LENGTH rather than by row or column?
expectedConcepts: dp[i][j] depends on strictly shorter intervals inside it
iterating by row would read entries that have not been computed yet

concepts.prompt: How does the 'burst balloons' problem invert the usual partition thinking, and why is that necessary?
expectedConcepts: instead of choosing which balloon to burst first, you choose which one is burst LAST in each interval
that makes the interval's boundaries fixed and independent, which the first-burst framing does not

concepts.prompt: What structural property of a trie makes prefix-based queries (e.g. 'does any word start with this prefix') O(L) instead of O(n*L) for n words of length L?
expectedConcepts: each node represents a shared prefix; children branch per next character, so following a query string character by character directly walks matching prefixes without scanning unrelated words

concepts.prompt: What's the difference between marking 'end of word' at a trie node versus just checking if a node exists, and why is that distinction necessary?
expectedConcepts: a node existing only means some longer word passes through that prefix, not that the prefix itself is a complete word
an explicit end-of-word flag distinguishes 'prefix present' from 'exact word present'

concepts.prompt: What is the space complexity of a trie, and what dominates it?
expectedConcepts: O(total characters across all inserted words) nodes in the worst case
each node carries a child array or map, so a fixed 26-slot array can be wasteful on sparse tries where a hash map is leaner

concepts.prompt: How do you delete a word from a trie without breaking other words?
expectedConcepts: unset the end-of-word flag, then remove nodes bottom-up only while they have no children and are not themselves word endings
removing shared prefix nodes would delete other words

concepts.prompt: How do you support 'count words with this prefix' efficiently in a trie?
expectedConcepts: store a prefix counter at each node, incremented on insert along the path
the query then reads a single counter instead of traversing the subtree

concepts.prompt: How does a trie support counting distinct substrings of a string efficiently, conceptually?
expectedConcepts: insert every suffix of the string into a trie; the number of distinct substrings equals the number of nodes created (excluding the root), since each new node represents one new distinct prefix-of-a-suffix (i.e. substring)

concepts.prompt: Why is a trie well suited for prefix-matching-heavy applications like autocomplete, over a hash set of all words?
expectedConcepts: a hash set only answers exact membership; a trie naturally supports 'all words with this prefix' by just descending to the prefix's node and exploring its subtree

concepts.prompt: What is the complexity of building a suffix trie for distinct-substring counting, and why can it be prohibitive?
expectedConcepts: O(n^2) nodes for a string of length n, since it inserts all n suffixes
suffix automata or suffix arrays solve the same problem in O(n) or O(n log n)

concepts.prompt: Why does each newly created trie node correspond to exactly one distinct substring?
expectedConcepts: a node represents a unique path from the root, i.e. a unique prefix of some suffix, which is exactly a distinct substring
no two distinct substrings share a node, and no substring lacks one

concepts.prompt: How does a trie support wildcard search (e.g. '.' matching any character)?
expectedConcepts: on a wildcard, recurse into ALL existing children rather than one
turns lookup into a bounded DFS, so complexity degrades with the number of wildcards

concepts.prompt: What is a binary/bitwise trie, and how does it differ structurally from a character trie?
expectedConcepts: each node has at most 2 children (0 and 1 bits) instead of up to 26+ for characters
numbers are inserted bit by bit, typically from most significant to least significant bit

concepts.prompt: How does a bitwise trie find the maximum XOR pair (or maximum XOR with a given number) in better than O(n^2)?
expectedConcepts: for a query number, greedily walk the trie choosing the opposite bit at each level when available (to maximize that bit's contribution to XOR), falling back to the same bit only when the opposite path doesn't exist
achieves O(n * bitlength) instead of checking every pair

concepts.prompt: Why must numbers be inserted into a bitwise trie from the MOST significant bit first?
expectedConcepts: higher bits dominate the XOR value, so the greedy choice must be made at the most significant bit first
inserting least-significant-first would make the greedy descent meaningless

concepts.prompt: What is the complexity of maximum-XOR-pair via a bitwise trie, and what does it replace?
expectedConcepts: O(n * B) where B is the bit width (typically 32)
replaces the O(n^2) all-pairs comparison

concepts.prompt: How does the technique extend to 'maximum XOR with a constraint', such as only considering numbers <= some limit?
expectedConcepts: either sort queries and insert numbers incrementally as they become eligible (offline processing), or store subtree counts to prune ineligible branches during descent

concepts.prompt: Why does naive string matching run in O(n*m) worst case, and what idea do KMP and Z-function share to avoid that?
expectedConcepts: naive matching re-scans from scratch after every mismatch, discarding information about the partial match already found
both KMP and Z-function precompute information about the pattern's own internal repeated structure so a mismatch can skip ahead without re-checking already-known-matching characters

concepts.prompt: What does the KMP failure function (longest proper prefix which is also a suffix, LPS array) represent, and how is it used during matching?
expectedConcepts: LPS[i] = length of the longest proper prefix of pattern[0..i] that is also a suffix of it
on a mismatch, instead of restarting, shift the pattern using LPS to reuse the longest already-matched prefix as the new starting alignment

concepts.prompt: How does Rabin-Karp use hashing to achieve average-case fast substring search, and what's its worst-case weakness?
expectedConcepts: computes a rolling hash of each window of text and compares it to the pattern's hash in O(1) per shift (average case), only doing a full character comparison on a hash match
worst case degrades to O(n*m) if many spurious hash collisions occur (mitigated by a good hash function/modulus choice)

concepts.prompt: What is the Z-function, and how does Z[i] relate to pattern matching when the pattern is prepended to the text with a separator?
expectedConcepts: Z[i] = length of the longest substring starting at i that matches a prefix of the whole string
after forming pattern + separator + text, any position in the text portion where Z[i] equals the pattern's length marks a full pattern match

concepts.prompt: What are the time and space complexities of KMP, split between preprocessing and matching?
expectedConcepts: O(m) to build the LPS array, O(n) to scan the text, O(n + m) total
O(m) extra space for the LPS array

concepts.prompt: Why does the text pointer in KMP never move backward, and why does that matter?
expectedConcepts: the LPS array supplies enough information to realign the pattern without re-examining text characters
it guarantees each text character is inspected a bounded number of times, which is what makes it linear

concepts.prompt: What is a common LPS construction mistake, and what does 'proper prefix' exclude?
expectedConcepts: a proper prefix cannot be the entire string itself
forgetting that lets LPS[i] equal the full length, causing an infinite loop during matching

concepts.prompt: How does a rolling hash update in O(1) when the window shifts by one character?
expectedConcepts: subtract the outgoing character's weighted contribution, multiply by the base, then add the incoming character
avoids recomputing the hash over the whole window
